title: Machine Learning Basics: Learning a Function from Examples
oneLiner: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, features and labels, training vs inference, and why a model that aces its training data can still be useless.
keyTakeaway: Machine learning replaces hand-written rules with a function whose parameters are fitted to example data. The goal is never to score well on the examples you trained on; it is to do well on data the model has not seen. That is why you hold back validation and test data, and why a more flexible model is not automatically a better one: past a point it starts memorising noise (overfitting).
explanation:
In ordinary programming you write the rules: if the motor current is above 12 A for 3 seconds, raise an alarm. In machine learning (ML) you pick a family of functions with adjustable numbers in them, called parameters or weights, and let an algorithm choose those numbers so the function fits a set of examples. The inputs to the function are features (current, temperature, vibration level), and in supervised learning each example also carries the right answer, its label ("bearing failed within a week" or not).

There are three broad kinds of learning. Supervised learning learns from labelled examples: classification predicts a category (spam or not, defect or not) and regression predicts a number (remaining useful life in hours). Unsupervised learning gets no labels and looks for structure on its own, such as clustering similar machines together or flagging readings that do not look like the rest (anomaly detection). Reinforcement learning has an agent take actions in an environment and receive a reward, and it learns a policy that earns more reward over time; it is how game-playing systems are trained, and a version of it is used to tune language models, as a later lesson shows. Many real systems mix these; large language models, for example, are pretrained with a self-supervised objective where the labels come free from the text itself (the next word).

Training is the expensive, one-off phase where the parameters are fitted. Inference is using the finished model to make a prediction, which happens every time someone calls it. When you use an AI coding tool you are only ever doing inference; nothing you type changes the model's weights in that moment.

The central danger is overfitting. A model with enough parameters can fit its training examples perfectly, including their noise and quirks, and then fail on anything new. The opposite, underfitting, is a model too simple to capture the real pattern. To tell them apart you split your data: a training set to fit the parameters, a validation set to compare models and tune settings (hyperparameters such as the polynomial degree below), and a test set you touch once at the end to estimate real-world performance. If you keep tuning against the test set it quietly becomes another validation set and stops being an honest estimate. Common splits are around 70/15/15 or 80/10/10, and the split must respect time and grouping: if the model will predict next month's failures, validate on data from after the training period, not a random shuffle.

The demo fits polynomials to 12 noisy training points drawn from a smooth curve, then measures error on separate validation points. Low degrees underfit. Around degree 3 to 5 both errors are low. Push the degree up and training error keeps falling while validation error climbs: the curve bends wildly to pass through every training point. Regularisation (penalising large weights) and more data are the usual cures. The data is generated from a fixed seed, so the numbers are the same every time.
